q: A bare granite dome above one Cape town gleams after rain, and both the town and its district take their name from it. Which district?
exp: Paarl means pearl in Dutch, and the outcrop is among the largest granite domes anywhere. The district is warmer and further from the sea than Stellenbosch, which pushes it toward Rhone varieties, Chenin Blanc and the fortified styles that gave Boberg its reason to exist.

q: Summer temperatures climb several degrees on the short drive inland from Stellenbosch to Paarl. What accounts for the jump?
opts: Paarl lies considerably closer to the equator
Paarl receives no winter rainfall to cool its soils
Paarl stands several hundred metres higher
Paarl lies further from the cold sea air
exp: Distance from the ocean is the strongest single variable in the Cape, and it changes faster than latitude ever could over twenty kilometres. The two districts share a border and a mountain, and still make quite different wine from the same grapes.

q: A white grape that once covered the great majority of Cape vineyards now survives chiefly in a handful of old blocks around Franschhoek. Which grape?
exp: Cape growers called it groendruif, the green grape, for the colour of its leaves, and in the nineteenth century it was very nearly the whole white vineyard. It collapsed to a fraction of the plantings during the twentieth, and the surviving old vines are treated as heritage material.

q: Vine nurseries cluster in one district at the foot of Bain's Kloof, and most of the country's grafted planting material starts life there. Which district?
exp: Almost every new Cape vineyard is planted with vines raised in that one valley, which makes its nurseries quietly influential over what the country grows. The district also makes ripe reds and Chenin Blanc in its own right, in a climate close to Paarl's.

q: One mountain lends its name to a ward in Stellenbosch and to a second ward in Paarl, on opposite flanks of the same slope. Which mountain?
exp: Simonsberg-Stellenbosch and Simonsberg-Paarl share a mountain and a reputation for serious red wine, and the district boundary rather than the geology decides which name a grower may use. It is a neat demonstration that a ward is drawn on the land and a district on the map.

q: Wheat fields, rolling hills and unirrigated bush vines lie an hour north of Cape Town, in a district named for the dark colour its native scrub takes on. Which district?
exp: Swartland means black land, after the renosterbos that darkens the hills. It was farmed for grain and bulk wine for most of its history, and dry farming is the norm rather than a boast there, since outside the Berg River corridor on its eastern edge there is next to no water to irrigate with.

q: Old dryland bush vines turned a bulk-farming district into the Cape's most closely watched source of fine wine over the last two decades. Which two varieties lead it?
opts: Chenin Blanc for the whites and Syrah for the reds
Colombard for the whites and Pinotage for the reds
Chardonnay for the whites and Cabernet Sauvignon for the reds
Sauvignon Blanc for the whites and Pinot Noir for the reds
exp: Chenin was already in the ground as old unirrigated bush vines, planted for bulk wine and brandy and then rediscovered, while the Syrah is largely modern planting, put on shale and granite from the 1990s by growers who had seen what the district could do. The reds are usually blended in the southern Rhone manner with Grenache, Mourvedre and Cinsaut, and the whites are picked earlier and handled far more gently than the district's history would suggest.

q: Stellenbosch, Swartland and Darling are neighbouring districts gathered under a single regional name. Which region?
exp: Paarl, Wellington, Tulbagh and Cape Town belong to it as well, so a blend drawn across any of them still has a legal place name to print. The name is inherited rather than descriptive, and several districts genuinely on the coast are not in it.

q: Cold Atlantic air reaches a small west coast district whose Groenekloof ward built a name for pungent, high-acid Sauvignon Blanc. Which district?
exp: The sea is close and the water is cold, so the mornings are foggy and the afternoons breezy even in midsummer. It sits immediately west of the Swartland and makes a completely different sort of wine because of that one difference.

q: Follow the coast road north beyond the Swartland and vineyards continue up a river valley long known for volume, and now also for old Grenache high on the mountain slopes above it. Which region?
exp: The valley floor is hot and irrigated and was built around co-operatives, but the Citrusdal Mountain district climbs several hundred metres above it, and the Piekenierskloof ward up there holds very old bush-vine Grenache. Altitude changed the region's reputation without changing its address.

q: Vines went into the slopes behind Cape Town in the 1680s on a governor's own farm, and the ward there is the oldest named wine origin in the country. Which ward?
exp: The original farm was later broken up, which is why several neighbouring estates carry versions of the name. The slopes are decomposed granite, face the incoming south-easter, and catch well over a metre of rain a year, which is a great deal by Cape standards.

q: No spirit is added and no noble rot is involved, yet the Cape's most historic sweet wine reaches enormous sugar levels from fruit shrivelled on the vine. Which variety supplies it?
exp: Muscat de Frontignan is the Cape name for the small-berried white Muscat, the grape the Cape also fortifies as Muscadel, and Muscat of Alexandria, which the Cape calls Hanepoot, is the coarser cousin grown for the table and for sweet fortified jerepigo. Production lapsed after phylloxera and the wine was revived in the 1980s, and its unusual distinction is that it concentrates by drying on the vine rather than by fungus or fortification.

q: Morning fog off the cold Atlantic settles over hills at the edge of Cape Town's northern suburbs, where deep red clay grows sharply defined Sauvignon Blanc. Which ward?
exp: The hills are low but they sit directly in the path of sea air, and the clay holds enough water for dry farming. It is a reminder that in the Cape a cool site is made by the ocean or by height, never by going further south.

q: The ward that gave the Cape its famous sweet wine is better known today for a dry white grown on cool granite slopes. Which grape?
exp: It is often bottled with a proportion of Semillon, in the Bordeaux manner rather than the Loire one, which gives it weight to carry the acidity. The sweet wine is still made, but it is a specialty of a couple of estates while the dry white is the ward's everyday business.

q: A valley running inland from a whale-watching town on the south coast has become the country's reference point for Pinot Noir. What is that valley called?
exp: The name means heaven and earth, and three separate wards climb it as the land rises away from the sea. All three sit inside the Walker Bay district, and the higher and further inland they go the later they pick.

q: Vineyards around Hermanus ripen slowly because of the cold water in the bay below them. Which district covers them?
exp: Cold water a few kilometres away holds the growing season long and the acidity high, which is why Pinot Noir and Chardonnay work there and Cabernet Sauvignon does not. Overberg and Cape Agulhas are genuine neighbouring districts in the same region.
